meta.title: Who really said "To me, there are three things everyone should do every day"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jim Valvano, at the first ESPY Awards on 4 March 1993 — but he said ‘we all should do every day’. Two transcripts agree; ‘everyone’ is a later drift.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To me, there are three things everyone should do every day'?
meta.ogDescription: The speaker and the speech are right. The wording is not: the transcripts read ‘three things we all should do every day’.

answer.label: Jim Valvano — but he said ‘we all’, not ‘everyone’
answer.authorDates: 1946–1993 · American college basketball coach and broadcaster
answer.sourceLine: Not as it is usually quoted. The speaker, the speech and the date are all correct — this is Jim Valvano, accepting the inaugural Arthur Ashe Courage and Humanitarian Award at the first ESPY Awards on 4 March 1993, eight weeks before he died of cancer. What drifted is one phrase. Every transcript we could read gives the sentence as ‘To me, there are three things we all should do every day’, and the version in circulation swaps in ‘everyone’. The thought is genuinely his; the quotation marks are what this page is about.

source.heading: What Valvano actually said

docMeta.dd: The first ESPY Awards, Madison Square Garden, New York
The inaugural Arthur Ashe Courage and Humanitarian Award

source.excerpt: To me, there are three things we all should do every day. We should do this every day of our lives. Number one is laugh. You should laugh every day. Number two is think. You should spend some time in thought. Number three is you should have your emotions moved to tears, could be happiness or joy. But think about it. If you laugh, you think and you cry, that’s a full day.
trail: A wording question is only ever settled by a transcript. Two of them, published independently of each other, carry this passage — and both read ‘there are three things we all should do every day’ Speakola’s transcript ↗
James Clear’s speech archive prints the same passage word for word, down to the closing line — ‘If you laugh, you think, and you cry, that’s a full day’ a second, independent transcript ↗

The occasion is not in doubt. Valvano spoke at the first ESPY Awards at Madison Square Garden on Thursday 4 March 1993, accepting the inaugural Arthur Ashe Courage and Humanitarian Award, and used the speech to announce the V Foundation for Cancer Research the speech, the award and the date ↗

One caution for anyone sourcing this speech: the transcript pages do not agree on when it happened. Speakola’s own header dates it 3 March 1993 and places it in Los Angeles. The ceremony was on 4 March 1993 at Madison Square Garden in New York, and that is the date this page uses the first ESPY ceremony ↗
source.excerptNote: The difference is one phrase, and it is the whole of this page: we all against everyone. It is a small drift and an easy one — the two mean the same thing — but a quotation that has been repaired for rhythm is no longer a quotation. Note also that the popular short form usually stops at ‘moved to tears’ and drops the line Valvano built the whole passage toward: if you laugh, you think and you cry, that’s a full day.
source.rightsNote: This is a 1993 speech, so it is well inside United States copyright and will be for decades yet — there is no public-domain claim to make here. Copyright in the words would rest with Valvano’s estate; ESPN separately holds the television broadcast the speech is usually watched in. Quoting a passage with attribution, as this page does, is ordinary practice; reproducing the speech whole is a different question. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Jim Valvano
author.heading: About Jim Valvano
author.metaLine: 1946–1993 · college basketball coach, broadcaster, founder of the V Foundation
author.bio: Jim Valvano coached North Carolina State to the 1983 NCAA championship as heavy underdogs, in a final settled when Lorenzo Charles caught a team-mate’s desperate last-second shot short and dunked it as time expired. He later worked as a broadcaster. Diagnosed with metastatic cancer, he used his 4 March 1993 ESPY acceptance speech to announce the V Foundation for Cancer Research and gave it the motto Don’t Give Up … Don’t Ever Give Up. He died 55 days later, on 28 April 1993, aged 47.

misattribution.heading: The wording problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here. Valvano said this, on a stage, on a date we can name. What travelled is a slightly tidied version of his sentence, and the tidying is invisible unless you go back to a transcript.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Valvano was dying when he said it. He had been told his cancer had spread, he could not have known how few weeks were left, and he spent his time on a stage at Madison Square Garden setting out what a day should contain. That is why the sentence has the weight it does — it is not a wellness prescription, it is a man deciding out loud what is worth doing with the time he had.
The same speech announced the V Foundation for Cancer Research and gave it the motto Don’t Give Up … Don’t Ever Give Up. He died 55 days later.
context.detailsSummary: Getting this one right when you quote it
detailsBody: The sentence begins ‘To me, there are three things we all should do every day’ — not ‘everyone’.
The next sentence, almost always dropped, is ‘We should do this every day of our lives.’
The passage is built to land on its last line: ‘If you laugh, you think and you cry, that’s a full day.’ Quoting the three items without it stops one beat early.
The date is 4 March 1993 and the venue is Madison Square Garden, whatever a transcript page’s header says.
